text:
Moth and Gravel. Field Note 6. A
map should leave room for doubt.

An AI narrated edition of the
published note.

When a few points become a room,
give a little robot a way to

sense what is nearby, then put
its readings on a screen.

A few colored points become a
shape. Soon, it is tempting to

see a room. The display has made
a powerful suggestion from a

modest collection of readings.
That is the interesting part of

our Kitronik buggy experiment.
The machine has an ultrasonic

sensor, a pair of motors, and a
way to report what it has found.

Python tools give those reports
a form someone can look at.

Somewhere between the sensor and
the picture, a design question

appears. How much certainty
should a map be allowed to

borrow from its own appearance?
Leave the unseen space open. The

current firmware starts its grid
at a neutral prior. A cell has

not become an empty piece of
floor simply because nothing has

been drawn there. As scans
arrive, the map accumulates

evidence. Traversed parts of a
sensor beam receive free space

updates. It's end point receives
occupied space updates.

Confidence affects the
contribution. Overlapping

observations can strengthen or
revise the picture. The

distinction matters to the
person reading it. Free,

occupied, and undecided are
three different answers. A quiet

neutral region leaves the
question visible. Filling

everything with reassuring space
would make the picture easier to

like and harder to trust. O1,
free. Evidence of free space.

The stored value is below 80.
Observations have moved it

toward free. O2, unclassified. A
question remains. Values from 80

through 170 stay unclassified.
The starting value is 128.

O3, occupied. Evidence of an
obstacle. The stored value is

above 170. Observations have
moved it toward occupied.

Three classifications in the
current firmware. Explanatory

symbols and exact stored value
thresholds, rather than a

product screen or measured
probabilities. A classification

describes accumulated evidence.
It is not a guarantee about the

floor. In the Python scan
viewer, the neutral region

occupies most of the saved
example. In the camera overlay,

unclassified cells remain
unpainted, while free and

occupied classifications add
color. Those are two ways to let

uncertainty survive the drawing.
The drawing has a point of view.

A polar plot shows readings
around the sensor. A top-down

view turns them into a shape. An
occupancy grid shows accumulated

belief about space. The distance
profile makes individual

readings easier to compare. The
saved scan visualizer puts these

views beside each other. They
share an input, but each makes

something easier to notice. A
gap can be obvious in one and

disappear into the overall
impression of another. One saved

sample. Four ways to look. The
repository's Python renderer,

called offline, with its saved
12-point sample. This older

sample contains a 32 x 32 grid.
Current firmware defines 64 x

64. The sample's physical
capture origin is not

established. Open the full-size
figure.

That is useful. A companion view
can question the attractive one.

It also gives the display a
responsibility. The reader

should be able to understand
what the marks represent, which

frame they belong to, and
whether they came from a current

observation or a saved example.
The robot moves, and the room
should stay put.

The current grid belongs to a
world frame with an origin at

the start. The robot's estimated
position changes inside it.

Keeping the map in that frame
lets observations from different

positions accumulate into one
place. But position is part of

the estimate too. This
experiment uses motor time

kinematics with selective
heading correction. A camera

marker provides an another
estimate of where the robot

might be, connected to the map
through calibration. The overlay

can draw the two trails
together, making their

disagreement available to
inspect. The interesting design

opportunity is a display that
gives someone a way to notice

when the alignment deserves
another look. Let the picture

stay provisional. There is
pleasure in a little machine

slowly giving a space a shape.
Colors, rays, and a moving

marker can make an otherwise
difficult stream of numbers

approachable. The display earns
that pleasure when its limits

remain readable, where it has
evidence, where it has an

estimate, and where it still has
a question. That is what we

would test next. Ask someone to
point out the parts the robot

has not established. Ask which
position they believe and why.

Show an old reading beside a new
one. Watch what they infer from

a blank area. The map does not
have to settle every doubt. It

has to leave room for the useful
ones.
